Mayor of San Diego :: History :: chunk_0001
The position of mayor was created when San Diego was first incorporated on March 27, 1850. However, the city went bankrupt in 1852, only two years after incorporation. As a result of the bankruptcy, the State of California dissolved the government and replaced the mayor and city council with a [board of trustees](#Presidents_of_the_Board_of_Trustees).[[1]](#cite_note-Smythe_5-2-1) The mayoral position was later re-established with a new charter in 1887.[[2]](#cite_note-2) This charter was replaced with a permanent City Charter on May 6, 1889, using the [strong mayor](/wiki/Strong_mayor "Strong mayor") form of government.

In 1931, a new charter was adopted using a [council–manager government](/wiki/Council%E2%80%93manager_government "Council–manager government") with a citywide mayor as leader of the city council.

In November 2004, voters approved Proposition F, returning San Diego to the strong mayor form of government on a five-year trial basis. This was made permanent in June 2010 with the passage of Proposition D.[[3]](#cite_note-city_clerk-3)

:   Early fixed-program [computers](/wiki/Computer "Computer") in the 1940s were operated manually by entering small programs via [switches](/wiki/Switch "Switch") in order to load and run a series of programs. As [transistor](/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") technology evolved in the 1950s, [central processing units](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and user [terminals](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal") came into use by 1955. The [mainframe computer](/wiki/Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") model was devised, and [modems](/wiki/Modem "Modem"), such as the [Bell 101](/wiki/Bell_101_modem "Bell 101 modem"), allowed [digital data](/wiki/Digital_data "Digital data") to be transmitted over regular unconditioned [telephone lines](/wiki/Telephone_line "Telephone line") at low speeds by the late 1950s. These technologies made it possible to exchange data between [remote computers](/wiki/Remote_desktop_software "Remote desktop software"). However, a fixed-line link was still necessary; the point-to-point communication model did not allow for direct communication between any two arbitrary systems. In addition, the applications were specific and not general purpose. Examples included [SAGE](/wiki/Semi-Automatic_Ground_Environment "Semi-Automatic Ground Environment") (1958) and [SABRE](/wiki/Sabre_(travel_reservation_system) "Sabre (travel reservation system)") (1960).

In [Northeast India](/wiki/Northeast_India "Northeast India") a pidgin known as [Haflong Hindi](/wiki/Haflong_Hindi "Haflong Hindi") has developed as a *lingua franca* for the people living in [Haflong](/wiki/Haflong "Haflong"), [Assam](/wiki/Assam "Assam") who speak other languages natively.[[87]](#cite_note-88) In [Arunachal Pradesh](/wiki/Arunachal_Pradesh "Arunachal Pradesh"), Hindi emerged as a lingua franca among locals who speak over 50 dialects natively.[[88]](#cite_note-89)

Hindi is quite easy to understand for many [Pakistanis](/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), who speak Urdu, which, like Hindi, is a standard register of the Hindustani language; additionally, Indian media are widely viewed in Pakistan.[[89]](#cite_note-Gandapur2012-90)

A sizeable population in [Afghanistan](/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan"), especially in [Kabul](/wiki/Kabul "Kabul"), can also speak and understand Hindi-Urdu due to the popularity and influence of [Bollywood](/wiki/Bollywood "Bollywood") films, songs and actors in the region.[[90]](#cite_note-Hakala2012-91)[[91]](#cite_note-Krishnamurthy2013-92)
